transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hello, Doctor. It's nice to meet you. Well, my daughter actually drove me here today, which was lovely of her, though we hit simply dreadful traffic on the way over. They've been doing construction on that main road since... oh, it must be 1998? I remember because my late husband bought his blue Buick that year, such a boat of a car, and he hated getting dust on it. 

But anyway, you asked why I'm here. Well, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around the house. Fixing things, arranging the pantry, volunteering for just one more committee at the church. Speaking of the church, the spring bazaar was last weekend and I ended up making three dozen of my lemon bars because Margaret's arthritis is acting up, poor dear. She usually does the baking. 

But... yes, what brings me in is that even at 87, I just have a terribly hard time just sitting down and being still. I don't know why I can't just rest in my armchair like everyone else my age.
When you're sitting in your armchair, do you feel sad or down in your mood, or do you find that things you normally enjoy—like your hobbies or time with family—just don't bring you pleasure anymore?

Sad? Oh heavens, no. I wouldn't say I feel sad at all. I still love all my little projects and seeing my family. In fact, I was just trying to work on a cross-stitch for my youngest great-grandson while sitting in that armchair. 

It's a wonderful chair, by the way—a lovely floral wingback I found at an estate sale over on Maple Drive. The Henderson estate, I believe it was. They had the most magnificent collection of antique thimbles, just hundreds of them in these little wooden display cases, but I just bought the chair and a little silver tray. I actually polished that tray just yesterday... or was it Tuesday? Must have been Tuesday, because the mailman was running late and I was watching for him out the front window. He usually comes right at eleven, you know. 

But no, I don't feel down or blue in the slightest. I just can't seem to stay sitting in that lovely chair for more than a few minutes without popping back up to dust the tray or check the mail or what have you. So, no, I still enjoy my life quite a bit!
When you feel that urge to get up and move around, do you notice your heart racing, or do your hands shake, or do you feel sweaty or uncomfortable in your body?

My heart? Oh goodness, no, nothing like that. My heart is strong as a horse. I actually just saw my regular doctor, Dr. Evans, back in January—or maybe it was February? No, it was definitely January, right after that terrible ice storm that knocked out the power over on Elm Street. We had to use candles for two whole days, and I ended up burning through all my good beeswax tapers. They smelled just like fresh honey, which was lovely, but they drip so terribly if there's even the slightest draft in the hallway. 

But no, I don't get sweaty or shaky at all. My hands are still quite steady, thank heavens. You really must have steady hands for cross-stitching, you know. My mother taught me how to stitch when I was just a little girl. She had the most beautiful sewing box... solid cherry wood with these tiny little brass hinges. I think my sister Eleanor took it when she moved down to Florida in the seventies. Florida is just much too humid for me, speaking of sweating! 

So, no, I don't feel uncomfortable or panicky in my body or anything like that. I just... I just feel like I need to be up and doing something.

When you feel that urge to get up and move around, do you also notice that you're worried or anxious about something, or does it feel more like a physical restlessness without any particular worry on your mind?

Worried? Oh, heavens no. I don't really have anything to be anxious about these days. The house is paid for, the children are all settled... well, except for my grandson David, but he’s always been a bit of a rolling stone. He just moved to Seattle, actually. Or was it Portland? Somewhere out West where it rains all the time. I sent him a lovely yellow raincoat for his birthday, but I doubt he wears it. Young people today just don't seem to care about keeping dry, do they? They just walk right out in the drizzle in their sweatshirts. 

But no, it's not worry at all. It's just... well, it's just exactly like you said, a physical restlessness. Like when I'm at the senior center meetings, or trying to sit through the announcements at church. Pastor Miller is a dear, but his announcements can drag on for twenty minutes! I just get this terrible ants-in-my-chair feeling. I find myself shifting around, or I just have to stand up and go get a cup of coffee, or I start straightening the hymn books in the pew. The hymn books at our church are that lovely deep burgundy color, you know. They match the carpeting they put in back in 2012. I remember because the carpet layers made such a mess of the vestibule, we had to hold Sunday school in the basement for three weeks! But yes, I just have to move around to get through it. No worry, just... ants in my chair.
Are you currently taking any medications, particularly any that help with mood or anxiety?

Medications for my mood or anxiety? Oh, no, nothing like that. I really don't take much at all, just my daily vitamin and something for my blood pressure. Dr. Evans gave me that blood pressure pill... oh, it must have been five years ago now. They're these tiny little pink pills, shaped almost like a diamond. They're so hard to pick up if you drop them on the linoleum! My kitchen floor has this pattern, little pink and grey squares, very popular in the sixties. We put it in right after my husband got his promotion at the bank. He was so proud of that promotion. We celebrated by going to that nice Italian place downtown—Luigi's, I think it was called. They had the most wonderful garlic bread, wrapped in a little checkered napkin in a wicker basket. I haven't been downtown in ages, though. The traffic is just dreadful now with all that construction on Main Street. They've been digging up the road for months! But no, no mood pills or anything like that for me.
Has your doctor ever mentioned that you might have an overactive thyroid, or has anyone ever told you that your restlessness might be a side effect of a medical condition or medication?

My thyroid? Oh, no, Dr. Evans has never said a peep about my thyroid. He always checks my neck when I go in for my yearly physical, just presses right here under my chin. He has such warm hands, which is a blessing. You know, usually doctors have freezing cold hands! I remember Dr. Gable, the doctor my family went to when I was a little girl in the thirties—his stethoscope was like a solid block of ice! We used to just dread going to see him in the wintertime. Winter seemed so much harsher back then, didn't it? We would get these enormous snowdrifts all the way up to the parlor windows. My older brother Thomas and I would build these massive snow forts out by the big oak tree. Thomas was always so terribly bossy about how the snow had to be packed down just perfectly or the walls would cave in. He ended up becoming an architect, so I suppose that makes sense! He actually helped design the public library over in Springfield. They have a lovely botanical garden in Springfield, right next to the library. The tulips in the spring are just breathtaking, they import the bulbs all the way from Holland. 

But... oh, I'm sorry, what was it you were asking? Right, the thyroid and the pills. No, nobody has ever told me my fidgeting is from a medical condition or my blood pressure pill or anything like that. I've just always been a person who needs to be up and doing!

You mentioned you take a blood pressure pill—has Dr. Evans ever checked your blood pressure recently, and has it been well-controlled, or have there been any changes in how you're feeling since you started taking it?

Well, my blood pressure? Yes, Dr. Evans checks it every time I go in. He always puts that cuff on my arm and pumps it up tight. It pinches a little, but he says it's perfectly fine, right where it should be. I haven't noticed any changes since I started taking those little pink pills. Well, except that I have to make sure I take them with breakfast. I usually have a bowl of oatmeal with a few raisins. My mother always said oatmeal sticks to your ribs and keeps you going until lunchtime. She used to make it on the stovetop in this heavy cast-iron pot. It took forever, not like those instant packets they have nowadays. Have you tried those? They taste like cardboard if you ask me. I bought a box of the maple brown sugar ones when they were on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, but I ended up giving them to the food drive at church. Our church has a wonderful food pantry, you know. Mrs. Higgins runs it, and she is just a saint. She's been organizing it for at least fifteen years, ever since her husband passed away. He was a lovely man, played the organ on Sundays. He had the most magnificent booming voice when he sang the hymns. But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, yes, my blood pressure is just fine, and I feel perfectly normal with the pills.
Have you had any recent illnesses, infections, or fevers in the past few months—perhaps a cold, flu, or urinary tract infection—or any other health problems that seemed to come on suddenly?

Illnesses or fevers? Oh, no, nothing like that. I haven't had so much as a sniffle all winter. I'm very careful about washing my hands, you know. I use that nice antibacterial soap, the one that smells like lavender. My granddaughter bought me a whole set of it for Christmas, along with a matching lotion. She's such a thoughtful girl, always bringing me little gifts. She just started her first year of college over at the state university. She's studying to be a teacher, which I think is just wonderful. We need good teachers, don't we? When I was in school, I had a teacher named Miss Appleby. She taught third grade and she was the strictest woman you'd ever meet. If you didn't have your multiplication tables memorized, she'd make you write them out a hundred times on the chalkboard! The chalk dust used to get everywhere, all over my nice pleated skirts. My mother would be so annoyed when I came home covered in white dust. She used to scrub those skirts by hand in the sink with a bar of Fels-Naptha soap. You don't see Fels-Naptha much anymore, do you? It was the only thing that would get the grass stains out of my brother's trousers after he'd been playing baseball in the empty lot down the street. They paved over that lot years ago, put up a strip mall with a dry cleaner and a little bakery. The bakery has the most delightful lemon tarts... 

Oh, dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? But no, to answer your question, I haven't been sick at all. No colds, no flu, nothing sudden like that. I've been perfectly healthy.
When you're feeling this restless and need to be up and doing things, do you also notice that your thoughts seem to be racing or jumping from one thing to another very quickly?

Racing thoughts? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. My mind is just... well, it's just doing what it's supposed to do! I'm always thinking about what needs to be done next, like making sure the laundry is folded before the afternoon programs come on. I like to watch that game show with the spinning wheel, you know the one? The host is so charming, though he's getting a bit gray around the temples these days. It happens to the best of us, I suppose! I remember when my husband first started getting gray hair. He was only in his thirties, can you imagine? We used to joke that it was because he worked at the bank and had to deal with all those grumpy people complaining about their accounts. He was a teller for forty years, right down at the First National on Main Street. They gave him a beautiful gold watch when he retired. It had an inscription on the back... something about dedication and service. I keep it in my jewelry box now, the wooden one with the little mother-of-pearl flowers on the lid. I bought that box at a flea market in... oh, it must have been 1982. We took a trip up to Vermont to see the fall leaves. The colors were just spectacular that year, bright reds and oranges everywhere you looked. We stayed in a little bed and breakfast that smelled like cinnamon and apples...

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, my thoughts. No, they don't race or jump around. I just have a lot to do and a lot to think about, that's all!

When you're talking with people, do you find that words just seem to pour out of your mouth faster than usual, or that people sometimes have trouble keeping up with what you're saying? Or does your speech feel about the same as it always has?

Words pouring out? Well, I suppose I do like to talk, but I wouldn't say it's faster than usual. I've always been a chatty person! My mother used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. She had all sorts of funny little sayings like that. She grew up on a farm in Ohio, you see, so she had a lot of country wisdom. They raised chickens and had a big vegetable garden. She taught me how to can tomatoes when I was just a little girl. You have to boil them first to get the skins off, and then you pack them into those glass Mason jars. The ones with the two-piece lids, you know? You have to make sure the seal is tight, or else they'll spoil. I still have some jars in my pantry, though I don't do much canning these days. It's so much easier to just buy them at the supermarket. Although, the tomatoes at the store never taste quite as sweet as the ones you grow yourself. I tried growing a tomato plant on my balcony last summer, but the squirrels got to it before I could harvest a single one! Those little rascals are so clever. I saw one climbing right up the side of the brick wall... 

But, oh, my speech? Yes, well, I think it's just the same as always. People seem to understand me just fine, as long as they're listening!

You mentioned feeling restless at church during announcements and at senior center meetings. Does this restlessness happen mainly when you're in those specific situations, or do you feel just as restless at home in your own armchair when you're by yourself?

Well, it's mostly when I'm out, you know. Like at the senior center meetings or sitting through those long church announcements. I just get this... this ants-in-my-chair feeling. I have to shift around, or I'll stand up to get a cup of coffee, or maybe just straighten the papers on the table in front of me just to get through it. The coffee at the senior center is always so weak, though. It tastes like dishwater! I keep telling Mary—she's the one who organizes the refreshments—I tell her, "Mary, you need to use two scoops for that big percolator." But she insists on being frugal. She says the budget is tight this year because they had to fix the roof over the bingo hall. It was leaking right onto the caller's table! Can you imagine? Poor Mr. Henderson had to hold an umbrella while he was calling out the numbers. He's such a good sport about it, though. He used to be a mailman, so I suppose he's used to working in all kinds of weather. "Neither snow nor rain nor heat," isn't that how the saying goes? My nephew is a mailman, actually. Well, a letter carrier, they call them now. He walks five miles a day on his route. Keeps him very fit! He's always trying to get me to walk more, telling me I need to get my steps in...

But, oh, what were we talking about? The restlessness? Yes, well, it's mostly just when I have to sit still for those meetings and things. At home in my armchair, I can just get up and putter around whenever I please!

When you're at home alone in your armchair and you decide you really want to sit down and rest—maybe because you're tired or you're trying to watch a movie—do you find it difficult to stay seated, or can you actually relax and sit still when you choose to?

Well, that's just the thing, isn't it? That's actually what brought me in to see you. For the past year or so, even when I tell myself, "Eleanor, just sit down and rest your bones," I just... I can't seem to do it. I have a terrible time just sitting down and being still, even at 87! I feel like I'm always puttering around, fixing this, arranging that, or volunteering for just one more thing. I volunteered to bake three dozen cookies for the church bake sale last week. Snickerdoodles, they're my specialty. You have to roll them in cinnamon sugar before you bake them, and the secret is a little pinch of cream of tartar. It makes them nice and chewy! I used my mother's old mixing bowl, the big yellow ceramic one. It has a little chip on the rim from when my son knocked it against the sink when he was helping me bake back in... oh, it must have been 1965. He was just a little tyke then, always wanting to lick the spoon. He's a lawyer now, very busy, lives out in Seattle. It rains so much out there, I don't know how they stand it. I went to visit him once, and I had to buy a special raincoat just for the trip. It was bright yellow, like a canary! I felt a bit silly wearing it, but it certainly kept me dry. 

But yes, even when I try to watch a movie, I end up getting up to dust the television stand or fold a stray blanket. I just can't seem to stay put!

You mentioned this restlessness started about a year ago. Do you remember what was happening around that time—were there any changes in your health, any new medications your doctor started you on, or anything else significant that happened right before you started noticing this problem?

Well, let me think back... I suppose it's been especially noticeable for about a year and five months now. Yes, that sounds about right. It all started around the time those awful insurance bills started piling up, and then the roof on the back porch decided it needed replacing. You know how it is with these old houses, it's always something! First the roof, then the water heater... The man who came to fix the water heater was so polite, though. He took his boots off before coming into the kitchen, which I appreciated. Not many young people have manners like that anymore. He told me he was engaged to be married in June, and they were planning a honeymoon to Hawaii. I went to Hawaii once, back in the seventies with my late husband. We went to Maui, and oh, the pineapples! They were so sweet, nothing like the ones you get in the cans here. We took a boat tour and saw a whale jump right out of the water. It was the most magnificent thing. My husband took a picture, but it just looked like a big gray blur. He was never very good with a camera, bless his heart. He always forgot to take the lens cap off! 

But anyway, because of all those bills and repairs, I felt like I had to push myself into taking on more responsibilities at the senior center to keep my mind off the stress, you see. And that's when I really started noticing I just couldn't sit still anymore.

You mentioned you've been taking those little pink blood pressure pills for about five years now. Can you tell me—did this restless, ants-in-your-chair feeling start around the same time you began taking the blood pressure medication, or did it start much more recently, like within the past year or so?

Well, no, it wasn't the blood pressure pills. I've been taking those little pink ones for five years, like I said, and they never bothered me. Dr. Miller prescribed them—he retired last spring, you know. Moved down to Boca Raton to be near his daughter. She's a dental hygienist down there. I always wondered how people can stand looking at teeth all day, but I suppose someone has to do it. My grandson just got braces, the clear ones, so you can hardly tell he's wearing them unless the light hits him just right. They cost an absolute fortune, though! His mother—my daughter-in-law, Susan—was complaining about the orthodontist bill just last Sunday when they came over for pot roast. I make a very good pot roast, if I do say so myself. The trick is to sear the meat first, really get a good crust on it, and then let it simmer low and slow with carrots and those little pearl onions. 

But no, the restlessness... it's much more recent than the blood pressure pills. Like I was saying before, it's been about a year and five months. It really became noticeable when all those insurance bills hit and the porch roof needed fixing. That's what pushed me to take on all those extra duties at the senior center, just to keep busy, and that's when I realized I just couldn't sit still anymore.

Between the time you started taking those pink blood pressure pills five years ago and about a year and a half ago when this restlessness began, did anything else change with your health—did Dr. Evans start you on any new medications, or did you have any illnesses or hospitalizations during that time?

Let me think... between the blood pressure pills and the porch roof... no, I don't believe so. I didn't have any hospital stays or anything awful like that. And Dr. Evans hasn't given me anything new. He's such a sweet man, Dr. Evans. He always wears those little bow ties, you know? It reminds me of my father. My father was a history professor at the college, and he wouldn't be caught dead in a regular necktie. He always said they just got in the way when he was eating his soup! He loved a good bowl of minestrone. We used to go to this little Italian place on Main Street for his birthday every year. They had the most wonderful garlic bread, it came out in a little basket wrapped in a red and white checkered napkin. 

The restaurant closed down in... oh, it must have been 1998. They turned the building into a dry cleaner, which is a real shame, because the man who runs it uses far too much starch. I took a silk blouse there once, a beautiful emerald green one I bought for a Christmas party, and it came back stiff as a board! I had to wash it three times in the bathroom sink just to get it to drape right again. 

But what were we talking about? Oh, Dr. Evans and my health. Yes, no, I was perfectly fine during those years, just the usual aches and pains of getting older, but no new pills or sicknesses.

Over this past year and a half when you've been feeling this restless and puttering around, have you actually gotten more done than you normally would—like more projects completed, more volunteer work accomplished, more things checked off your list—or does it feel like you're just moving around without really getting extra things finished?

Well, that's a good question. You'd think with all this moving about I'd have the cleanest house in the county, wouldn't you? But no, not really. I'm always up and doing something, but it just feels like I'm spinning my wheels. I'll start organizing the hall closet, and then I'll find an old photo album, and before I know it, I'm sitting on the floor looking at pictures of my niece's wedding from 2004. It was a beautiful wedding, out in a garden with all these white roses. The bridesmaids wore lavender, which is a lovely color, but it washes some people out, don't you think? My sister—my niece's mother—insisted on it because it matched the invitations. She always was a stickler for coordination. When we were girls, she wouldn't even let her dolls wear mismatched shoes! She had this one doll, a Shirley Temple doll with those perfect little ringlets... oh, I loved that doll. 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm getting more done. I'm just puttering around, starting one thing and moving to another, and at the end of the day, the closet is still a mess and I'm just exhausted from all the pacing.
In the past year or two, have you ever had a fall, hit your head, had a stroke, or any kind of sudden neurological problem that a doctor told you about?

No, goodness no. I haven't fallen or hit my head, and certainly no strokes. My neighbor, though, Mr. Henderson—he had a stroke a few years back. It was terribly sad. He used to be out in his garden every single morning at 6 AM, rain or shine, tending to his tomatoes. He grew those big, beautiful heirloom ones, the ones that are sort of purple and green on the shoulders? Oh, they made the most wonderful sandwiches. Just a little mayonnaise, salt, and pepper on toasted sourdough. I used to buy my sourdough from that bakery on 4th Street, the one with the blue awning, but they closed down during the pandemic. Such a shame. The young couple who ran it were always so polite. The husband had this lovely singing voice, he'd hum while he kneaded the dough... 

But anyway, no, nothing like that for me. My head is perfectly fine, thank heavens. Just a bit too full of thoughts these days, I suppose!

Over this past year and a half when you've been feeling restless, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling more irritable or grumpy than usual, or have you felt more sad or down at any point, even if just occasionally?

Well, no, not really. I don't think I've been grumpy or sad. I'm usually a pretty cheerful person, you know? Even when things get a bit chaotic with all this pacing. Speaking of pacing, I was walking back and forth in the living room just yesterday, and I noticed the most peculiar thing about my curtains. They're these heavy velvet drapes I bought back in the seventies—a deep maroon color. Velvet was so popular then, wasn't it? Everyone had velvet couches and velvet pillows. My sister even had a crushed velvet pantsuit in mustard yellow. She wore it to a fondue party we hosted in '74. Fondue was all the rage! We had cheese fondue first, and then chocolate for dessert. We dipped little pieces of pound cake and strawberries into the chocolate. It was terribly messy, but oh, so much fun. 

But no, to answer your question, my mood has been just fine. No sadness or grumpiness at all. Just the restlessness, really.

When you have this restless feeling and need to move around, do you ever notice that your legs or feet feel like they have to move, or like there's an uncomfortable sensation in your legs that makes you want to shift or pace? Or does it feel more like a general urge to be active without any particular uncomfortable feeling in your body?

Well, no, it's not really an uncomfortable feeling in my legs. It's more just... a general feeling of needing to be doing something, you know? Like I just can't sit still. It's not like a cramp or a tingle or anything like that. Speaking of tingles, though, my feet used to fall asleep all the time when I'd sit on that old floral armchair we had in the den. It was a beautiful chair, really—had these big pink peonies on a cream background. I bought it at an estate sale over in Westlake. The woman running the sale was wearing the most fascinating brooch. It was shaped like a peacock, with real little emeralds for the eyes and sapphire tail feathers. I asked her about it, and she said it belonged to her great-aunt who used to travel all over Europe in the twenties. Imagine that! Traveling by ocean liner back then. They had those grand dining rooms with crystal chandeliers and a string quartet playing while you ate dinner. I've always wanted to go on a cruise, maybe up to Alaska to see the glaciers. I hear they're just breathtaking, though I suppose it would be terribly cold. You'd need a good, thick coat. My grandson bought me a lovely wool coat last Christmas, a deep forest green. It's so warm, but it's a bit heavy, to be honest. 

But anyway, no, my legs don't feel uncomfortable or anything. I just feel like I need to be up and moving around.

When you feel this urge to get up and move around, does it feel like something you absolutely have to do—like you can't resist it even if you tried—or does it feel more like you just prefer to be doing something rather than sitting still?

Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, really. I mean, I *could* sit still if I really forced myself, but it's just so much nicer to be doing something. It feels more like a preference, I think. I just don't like sitting idle. My mother was the exact same way, you know. She was always knitting or crocheting if she had to sit down. She made the most beautiful afghans. I still have the one she made for my wedding present—it's a lovely cream color with a sort of shell pattern. She used this very soft baby alpaca yarn she special-ordered from a catalog. Catalogs were so wonderful back then, weren't they? The Sears Roebuck catalog was thick as a telephone book! We used to circle the toys we wanted for Christmas in the Wish Book. I always wanted one of those Shirley Temple dolls with the little ringlets. My neighbor, little Patty, had one, and she had a whole wardrobe for it, little sailor dresses and patent leather shoes. The shoes even had tiny buckles! I don't know how they made things so small... 

But yes, to answer you, I just prefer to be up and about. It's not like I absolutely *have* to, I just... want to.

patient.answer:
Hello, Doctor. It's nice to meet you. Well, my daughter actually drove me here today, which was lovely of her, though we hit simply dreadful traffic on the way over. They've been doing construction on that main road since... oh, it must be 1998? I remember because my late husband bought his blue Buick that year, such a boat of a car, and he hated getting dust on it. 

But anyway, you asked why I'm here. Well, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around the house. Fixing things, arranging the pantry, volunteering for just one more committee at the church. Speaking of the church, the spring bazaar was last weekend and I ended up making three dozen of my lemon bars because Margaret's arthritis is acting up, poor dear. She usually does the baking. 

But... yes, what brings me in is that even at 87, I just have a terribly hard time just sitting down and being still. I don't know why I can't just rest in my armchair like everyone else my age.

inference.note: 87-year-old presenting with persistent inability to rest, constant need for activity, and difficulty with inactivity. Initial differential includes generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), major depressive disorder (F32.9), bipolar disorder (F31.9), anxiety disorder due to medical condition (F06.32), and nervousness/restlessness (R45.1). Patient's tangential speech and excessive detail-orientation noted. Need to assess mood, anxiety symptoms, medical comorbidities, and functional impact.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's restlessness and inability to sit still is accompanied by depressed mood, anhedonia, or other neurovegetative symptoms of depression, which would help differentiate F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder) from other candidates like generalized anxiety or adjustment issues.
doctor.question: When you're sitting in your armchair, do you feel sad or down in your mood, or do you find that things you normally enjoy—like your hobbies or time with family—just don't bring you pleasure anymore?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depression (feeling sad, down, or anhedonia), which are not covered in my symptom profile for ADHD.

patient.answer:
Sad? Oh heavens, no. I wouldn't say I feel sad at all. I still love all my little projects and seeing my family. In fact, I was just trying to work on a cross-stitch for my youngest great-grandson while sitting in that armchair. 

It's a wonderful chair, by the way—a lovely floral wingback I found at an estate sale over on Maple Drive. The Henderson estate, I believe it was. They had the most magnificent collection of antique thimbles, just hundreds of them in these little wooden display cases, but I just bought the chair and a little silver tray. I actually polished that tray just yesterday... or was it Tuesday? Must have been Tuesday, because the mailman was running late and I was watching for him out the front window. He usually comes right at eleven, you know. 

But no, I don't feel down or blue in the slightest. I just can't seem to stay sitting in that lovely chair for more than a few minutes without popping back up to dust the tray or check the mail or what have you. So, no, I still enjoy my life quite a bit!

inference.note: Ruled out F32.9 (major depressive disorder) and F31.9 (bipolar disorder) as patient denies mood symptoms and reports continued enjoyment of activities. The presentation is more consistent with anxiety disorder, organic mental disorder, or restlessness/agitation. Patient's tangential speech and difficulty with sustained attention also noted.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's restlessness is accompanied by physical anxiety symptoms (tremor, palpitations, sweating) that would suggest generalized anxiety disorder, versus pure psychomotor agitation from another cause, versus normal aging-related changes.
doctor.question: When you feel that urge to get up and move around, do you notice your heart racing, or do your hands shake, or do you feel sweaty or uncomfortable in your body?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical symptoms of anxiety (racing heart, shaking hands, sweating, physical discomfort), which are not covered by any of the ADHD symptom profile items provided.

patient.answer:
My heart? Oh goodness, no, nothing like that. My heart is strong as a horse. I actually just saw my regular doctor, Dr. Evans, back in January—or maybe it was February? No, it was definitely January, right after that terrible ice storm that knocked out the power over on Elm Street. We had to use candles for two whole days, and I ended up burning through all my good beeswax tapers. They smelled just like fresh honey, which was lovely, but they drip so terribly if there's even the slightest draft in the hallway. 

But no, I don't get sweaty or shaky at all. My hands are still quite steady, thank heavens. You really must have steady hands for cross-stitching, you know. My mother taught me how to stitch when I was just a little girl. She had the most beautiful sewing box... solid cherry wood with these tiny little brass hinges. I think my sister Eleanor took it when she moved down to Florida in the seventies. Florida is just much too humid for me, speaking of sweating! 

So, no, I don't feel uncomfortable or panicky in my body or anything like that. I just... I just feel like I need to be up and doing something.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's symptoms are better explained by generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) with physical restlessness, or by a medical/neurological condition (F06.32) such as akathisia or medication side effect, versus anxiety not otherwise specified (R45.1). Specifically, I need to clarify whether there is an internal sense of dread, worry, or fear accompanying the restlessness, or if it is purely motor/physical restlessness without emotional anxiety content.
doctor.question: When you feel that urge to get up and move around, do you also notice that you're worried or anxious about something, or does it feel more like a physical restlessness without any particular worry on your mind?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: When I'm at the senior center meetings or sitting through church announcements, I get this ants-in-my-chair feeling and have to shift around, stand up for coffee, or straighten papers just to get through it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the nature of the urge to get up and move around, specifically if it feels like a physical restlessness without particular worry, which directly maps to the feeling of restlessness (S012) described in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worried? Oh, heavens no. I don't really have anything to be anxious about these days. The house is paid for, the children are all settled... well, except for my grandson David, but he’s always been a bit of a rolling stone. He just moved to Seattle, actually. Or was it Portland? Somewhere out West where it rains all the time. I sent him a lovely yellow raincoat for his birthday, but I doubt he wears it. Young people today just don't seem to care about keeping dry, do they? They just walk right out in the drizzle in their sweatshirts. 

But no, it's not worry at all. It's just... well, it's just exactly like you said, a physical restlessness. Like when I'm at the senior center meetings, or trying to sit through the announcements at church. Pastor Miller is a dear, but his announcements can drag on for twenty minutes! I just get this terrible ants-in-my-chair feeling. I find myself shifting around, or I just have to stand up and go get a cup of coffee, or I start straightening the hymn books in the pew. The hymn books at our church are that lovely deep burgundy color, you know. They match the carpeting they put in back in 2012. I remember because the carpet layers made such a mess of the vestibule, we had to hold Sunday school in the basement for three weeks! But yes, I just have to move around to get through it. No worry, just... ants in my chair.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is a medication side effect (akathisia from antipsychotics) versus generalized anxiety disorder versus normal aging, by establishing current medication use
doctor.question: Are you currently taking any medications, particularly any that help with mood or anxiety?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about current medications, which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: Medications for my mood or anxiety? Oh, no, nothing like that. I really don't take much at all, just my daily vitamin and something for my blood pressure. Dr. Evans gave me that blood pressure pill... oh, it must have been five years ago now. They're these tiny little pink pills, shaped almost like a diamond. They're so hard to pick up if you drop them on the linoleum! My kitchen floor has this pattern, little pink and grey squares, very popular in the sixties. We put it in right after my husband got his promotion at the bank. He was so proud of that promotion. We celebrated by going to that nice Italian place downtown—Luigi's, I think it was called. They had the most wonderful garlic bread, wrapped in a little checkered napkin in a wicker basket. I haven't been downtown in ages, though. The traffic is just dreadful now with all that construction on Main Street. They've been digging up the road for months! But no, no mood pills or anything like that for me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is a side effect of a medical condition or medication (suggesting F06.32) versus a primary anxiety disorder (F41.1) versus generalized anxiety in an older adult (R45.1). Need to clarify if there's an underlying medical cause like hyperthyroidism, akathisia from medication, or other organic etiology.
doctor.question: Has your doctor ever mentioned that you might have an overactive thyroid, or has anyone ever told you that your restlessness might be a side effect of a medical condition or medication?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about potential medical conditions like an overactive thyroid or side effects from medication that might cause the restlessness. This is a rule-out question for medical conditions and is not covered by the psychiatric symptom profiles provided.

patient.answer:
My thyroid? Oh, no, Dr. Evans has never said a peep about my thyroid. He always checks my neck when I go in for my yearly physical, just presses right here under my chin. He has such warm hands, which is a blessing. You know, usually doctors have freezing cold hands! I remember Dr. Gable, the doctor my family went to when I was a little girl in the thirties—his stethoscope was like a solid block of ice! We used to just dread going to see him in the wintertime. Winter seemed so much harsher back then, didn't it? We would get these enormous snowdrifts all the way up to the parlor windows. My older brother Thomas and I would build these massive snow forts out by the big oak tree. Thomas was always so terribly bossy about how the snow had to be packed down just perfectly or the walls would cave in. He ended up becoming an architect, so I suppose that makes sense! He actually helped design the public library over in Springfield. They have a lovely botanical garden in Springfield, right next to the library. The tulips in the spring are just breathtaking, they import the bulbs all the way from Holland. 

But... oh, I'm sorry, what was it you were asking? Right, the thyroid and the pills. No, nobody has ever told me my fidgeting is from a medical condition or my blood pressure pill or anything like that. I've just always been a person who needs to be up and doing!

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is a primary anxiety disorder (F41.1) versus a medical condition (F06.32) by assessing whether there are any other anxiety symptoms like worry, tension, or panic that might not have been fully captured, or to rule out organic causes by asking about recent medical changes
doctor.question: You mentioned you take a blood pressure pill—has Dr. Evans ever checked your blood pressure recently, and has it been well-controlled, or have there been any changes in how you're feeling since you started taking it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's blood pressure control and any changes since starting the medication, which is related to medical history and not covered by the psychiatric symptom profile.

patient.answer: Well, my blood pressure? Yes, Dr. Evans checks it every time I go in. He always puts that cuff on my arm and pumps it up tight. It pinches a little, but he says it's perfectly fine, right where it should be. I haven't noticed any changes since I started taking those little pink pills. Well, except that I have to make sure I take them with breakfast. I usually have a bowl of oatmeal with a few raisins. My mother always said oatmeal sticks to your ribs and keeps you going until lunchtime. She used to make it on the stovetop in this heavy cast-iron pot. It took forever, not like those instant packets they have nowadays. Have you tried those? They taste like cardboard if you ask me. I bought a box of the maple brown sugar ones when they were on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, but I ended up giving them to the food drive at church. Our church has a wonderful food pantry, you know. Mrs. Higgins runs it, and she is just a saint. She's been organizing it for at least fifteen years, ever since her husband passed away. He was a lovely man, played the organ on Sundays. He had the most magnificent booming voice when he sang the hymns. But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, yes, my blood pressure is just fine, and I feel perfectly normal with the pills.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any recent medical events, infections, or acute illness that could explain akathisia as a medical symptom (F06.32) versus primary generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1) or anxiety unspecified (R45.1)
doctor.question: Have you had any recent illnesses, infections, or fevers in the past few months—perhaps a cold, flu, or urinary tract infection—or any other health problems that seemed to come on suddenly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recent illnesses, infections, or fevers (e.g., cold, flu, UTI) or sudden health problems to rule out medical causes for the symptoms. This does not correspond to any of the ADHD symptom criteria or other profile items.

patient.answer:
Illnesses or fevers? Oh, no, nothing like that. I haven't had so much as a sniffle all winter. I'm very careful about washing my hands, you know. I use that nice antibacterial soap, the one that smells like lavender. My granddaughter bought me a whole set of it for Christmas, along with a matching lotion. She's such a thoughtful girl, always bringing me little gifts. She just started her first year of college over at the state university. She's studying to be a teacher, which I think is just wonderful. We need good teachers, don't we? When I was in school, I had a teacher named Miss Appleby. She taught third grade and she was the strictest woman you'd ever meet. If you didn't have your multiplication tables memorized, she'd make you write them out a hundred times on the chalkboard! The chalk dust used to get everywhere, all over my nice pleated skirts. My mother would be so annoyed when I came home covered in white dust. She used to scrub those skirts by hand in the sink with a bar of Fels-Naptha soap. You don't see Fels-Naptha much anymore, do you? It was the only thing that would get the grass stains out of my brother's trousers after he'd been playing baseball in the empty lot down the street. They paved over that lot years ago, put up a strip mall with a dry cleaner and a little bakery. The bakery has the most delightful lemon tarts... 

Oh, dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? But no, to answer your question, I haven't been sick at all. No colds, no flu, nothing sudden like that. I've been perfectly healthy.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is accompanied by racing thoughts or flight of ideas, which would suggest a manic/hypomanic state (F41.1 - Generalized Anxiety Disorder with prominent physical symptoms vs F06.32 - Mood disorder due to medical condition vs R45.1 - Nervousness). The patient's tangential speech and excessive detail-giving could indicate racing thoughts rather than just anxiety or a medical condition.
doctor.question: When you're feeling this restless and need to be up and doing things, do you also notice that your thoughts seem to be racing or jumping from one thing to another very quickly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about racing thoughts or flight of ideas, which is typically a symptom of mania. My symptom profile for ADHD does not include racing thoughts.

patient.answer:
Racing thoughts? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. My mind is just... well, it's just doing what it's supposed to do! I'm always thinking about what needs to be done next, like making sure the laundry is folded before the afternoon programs come on. I like to watch that game show with the spinning wheel, you know the one? The host is so charming, though he's getting a bit gray around the temples these days. It happens to the best of us, I suppose! I remember when my husband first started getting gray hair. He was only in his thirties, can you imagine? We used to joke that it was because he worked at the bank and had to deal with all those grumpy people complaining about their accounts. He was a teller for forty years, right down at the First National on Main Street. They gave him a beautiful gold watch when he retired. It had an inscription on the back... something about dedication and service. I keep it in my jewelry box now, the wooden one with the little mother-of-pearl flowers on the lid. I bought that box at a flea market in... oh, it must have been 1982. We took a trip up to Vermont to see the fall leaves. The colors were just spectacular that year, bright reds and oranges everywhere you looked. We stayed in a little bed and breakfast that smelled like cinnamon and apples...

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, my thoughts. No, they don't race or jump around. I just have a lot to do and a lot to think about, that's all!

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is accompanied by pressured speech or flight of ideas, which would suggest a manic/hypomanic state (F41.1 Generalized Anxiety Disorder vs F06.32 Mood disorder due to medical condition vs R45.1 Nervousness). The patient has shown tangential speech but I need to clarify if this reflects racing thoughts/pressured speech or is simply her baseline personality. This distinction is critical for separating bipolar disorder from anxiety or medical causes.
doctor.question: When you're talking with people, do you find that words just seem to pour out of your mouth faster than usual, or that people sometimes have trouble keeping up with what you're saying? Or does your speech feel about the same as it always has?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about pressured speech, which is a symptom of mania or hypomania. My symptom profile covers ADHD symptoms like blurting out answers, but it does not include pressured speech.

patient.answer:
Words pouring out? Well, I suppose I do like to talk, but I wouldn't say it's faster than usual. I've always been a chatty person! My mother used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. She had all sorts of funny little sayings like that. She grew up on a farm in Ohio, you see, so she had a lot of country wisdom. They raised chickens and had a big vegetable garden. She taught me how to can tomatoes when I was just a little girl. You have to boil them first to get the skins off, and then you pack them into those glass Mason jars. The ones with the two-piece lids, you know? You have to make sure the seal is tight, or else they'll spoil. I still have some jars in my pantry, though I don't do much canning these days. It's so much easier to just buy them at the supermarket. Although, the tomatoes at the store never taste quite as sweet as the ones you grow yourself. I tried growing a tomato plant on my balcony last summer, but the squirrels got to it before I could harvest a single one! Those little rascals are so clever. I saw one climbing right up the side of the brick wall... 

But, oh, my speech? Yes, well, I think it's just the same as always. People seem to understand me just fine, as long as they're listening!

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is a primary anxiety disorder (F41.1) versus a medical condition (F06.32) or adjustment disorder (R45.1) by assessing if there are specific triggers or situations that provoke the anxiety/restlessness, versus it being generalized and constant
doctor.question: You mentioned feeling restless at church during announcements and at senior center meetings. Does this restlessness happen mainly when you're in those specific situations, or do you feel just as restless at home in your own armchair when you're by yourself?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: When I'm at the senior center meetings or sitting through church announcements, I get this ants-in-my-chair feeling and have to shift around, stand up for coffee, or straighten papers just to get through it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my feelings of restlessness at church and senior center meetings, which directly corresponds to my symptom of feeling restless in inappropriate situations.

patient.answer:
Well, it's mostly when I'm out, you know. Like at the senior center meetings or sitting through those long church announcements. I just get this... this ants-in-my-chair feeling. I have to shift around, or I'll stand up to get a cup of coffee, or maybe just straighten the papers on the table in front of me just to get through it. The coffee at the senior center is always so weak, though. It tastes like dishwater! I keep telling Mary—she's the one who organizes the refreshments—I tell her, "Mary, you need to use two scoops for that big percolator." But she insists on being frugal. She says the budget is tight this year because they had to fix the roof over the bingo hall. It was leaking right onto the caller's table! Can you imagine? Poor Mr. Henderson had to hold an umbrella while he was calling out the numbers. He's such a good sport about it, though. He used to be a mailman, so I suppose he's used to working in all kinds of weather. "Neither snow nor rain nor heat," isn't that how the saying goes? My nephew is a mailman, actually. Well, a letter carrier, they call them now. He walks five miles a day on his route. Keeps him very fit! He's always trying to get me to walk more, telling me I need to get my steps in...

But, oh, what were we talking about? The restlessness? Yes, well, it's mostly just when I have to sit still for those meetings and things. At home in my armchair, I can just get up and putter around whenever I please!

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is situational (only in structured/constrained settings) or pervasive (also present at home when she wants to sit still), which would help differentiate between anxiety disorder (F41.1) and akathisia from medication (F06.32) versus generalized restlessness
doctor.question: When you're at home alone in your armchair and you decide you really want to sit down and rest—maybe because you're tired or you're trying to watch a movie—do you find it difficult to stay seated, or can you actually relax and sit still when you choose to?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that for the past year or so I feel like I’m always puttering, fixing, arranging, or volunteering for one more thing, and even at 87 I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have difficulty sitting down and being still when I want to relax at home, which directly matches my symptom of having a hard time just sitting down and being still, as described in S014.

patient.answer:
Well, that's just the thing, isn't it? That's actually what brought me in to see you. For the past year or so, even when I tell myself, "Eleanor, just sit down and rest your bones," I just... I can't seem to do it. I have a terrible time just sitting down and being still, even at 87! I feel like I'm always puttering around, fixing this, arranging that, or volunteering for just one more thing. I volunteered to bake three dozen cookies for the church bake sale last week. Snickerdoodles, they're my specialty. You have to roll them in cinnamon sugar before you bake them, and the secret is a little pinch of cream of tartar. It makes them nice and chewy! I used my mother's old mixing bowl, the big yellow ceramic one. It has a little chip on the rim from when my son knocked it against the sink when he was helping me bake back in... oh, it must have been 1965. He was just a little tyke then, always wanting to lick the spoon. He's a lawyer now, very busy, lives out in Seattle. It rains so much out there, I don't know how they stand it. I went to visit him once, and I had to buy a special raincoat just for the trip. It was bright yellow, like a canary! I felt a bit silly wearing it, but it certainly kept me dry. 

But yes, even when I try to watch a movie, I end up getting up to dust the television stand or fold a stray blanket. I just can't seem to stay put!

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is a primary symptom (akathisia/anxiety disorder) or secondary to an underlying medical/neurological condition by asking about onset and temporal relationship to any medical events or medication changes
doctor.question: You mentioned this restlessness started about a year ago. Do you remember what was happening around that time—were there any changes in your health, any new medications your doctor started you on, or anything else significant that happened right before you started noticing this problem?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It has been especially noticeable for about a year and five months, since the insurance bills and home repairs pushed me into taking on more at the senior center.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of the restlessness starting and what significant events or changes happened around that time, which directly corresponds to the duration and the specific triggers mentioned in the profile.

patient.answer:
Well, let me think back... I suppose it's been especially noticeable for about a year and five months now. Yes, that sounds about right. It all started around the time those awful insurance bills started piling up, and then the roof on the back porch decided it needed replacing. You know how it is with these old houses, it's always something! First the roof, then the water heater... The man who came to fix the water heater was so polite, though. He took his boots off before coming into the kitchen, which I appreciated. Not many young people have manners like that anymore. He told me he was engaged to be married in June, and they were planning a honeymoon to Hawaii. I went to Hawaii once, back in the seventies with my late husband. We went to Maui, and oh, the pineapples! They were so sweet, nothing like the ones you get in the cans here. We took a boat tour and saw a whale jump right out of the water. It was the most magnificent thing. My husband took a picture, but it just looked like a big gray blur. He was never very good with a camera, bless his heart. He always forgot to take the lens cap off! 

But anyway, because of all those bills and repairs, I felt like I had to push myself into taking on more responsibilities at the senior center to keep my mind off the stress, you see. And that's when I really started noticing I just couldn't sit still anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is akathisia (medication side effect) by establishing the exact timeline of when the blood pressure medication was started relative to when the restlessness began
doctor.question: You mentioned you've been taking those little pink blood pressure pills for about five years now. Can you tell me—did this restless, ants-in-your-chair feeling start around the same time you began taking the blood pressure medication, or did it start much more recently, like within the past year or so?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It has been especially noticeable for about a year and five months, since the insurance bills and home repairs pushed me into taking on more at the senior center.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of when the restless symptoms started to clarify the duration and rule out medication side effects.

patient.answer:
Well, no, it wasn't the blood pressure pills. I've been taking those little pink ones for five years, like I said, and they never bothered me. Dr. Miller prescribed them—he retired last spring, you know. Moved down to Boca Raton to be near his daughter. She's a dental hygienist down there. I always wondered how people can stand looking at teeth all day, but I suppose someone has to do it. My grandson just got braces, the clear ones, so you can hardly tell he's wearing them unless the light hits him just right. They cost an absolute fortune, though! His mother—my daughter-in-law, Susan—was complaining about the orthodontist bill just last Sunday when they came over for pot roast. I make a very good pot roast, if I do say so myself. The trick is to sear the meat first, really get a good crust on it, and then let it simmer low and slow with carrots and those little pearl onions. 

But no, the restlessness... it's much more recent than the blood pressure pills. Like I was saying before, it's been about a year and five months. It really became noticeable when all those insurance bills hit and the porch roof needed fixing. That's what pushed me to take on all those extra duties at the senior center, just to keep busy, and that's when I realized I just couldn't sit still anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is a primary symptom or secondary to another medical condition by establishing timeline correlation with any acute medical events or medication changes
doctor.question: Between the time you started taking those pink blood pressure pills five years ago and about a year and a half ago when this restlessness began, did anything else change with your health—did Dr. Evans start you on any new medications, or did you have any illnesses or hospitalizations during that time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical history, new medications, illnesses, or hospitalizations to rule out other causes for the restlessness. This is not covered by any of the specific ADHD symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Let me think... between the blood pressure pills and the porch roof... no, I don't believe so. I didn't have any hospital stays or anything awful like that. And Dr. Evans hasn't given me anything new. He's such a sweet man, Dr. Evans. He always wears those little bow ties, you know? It reminds me of my father. My father was a history professor at the college, and he wouldn't be caught dead in a regular necktie. He always said they just got in the way when he was eating his soup! He loved a good bowl of minestrone. We used to go to this little Italian place on Main Street for his birthday every year. They had the most wonderful garlic bread, it came out in a little basket wrapped in a red and white checkered napkin. 

The restaurant closed down in... oh, it must have been 1998. They turned the building into a dry cleaner, which is a real shame, because the man who runs it uses far too much starch. I took a silk blouse there once, a beautiful emerald green one I bought for a Christmas party, and it came back stiff as a board! I had to wash it three times in the bathroom sink just to get it to drape right again. 

But what were we talking about? Oh, Dr. Evans and my health. Yes, no, I was perfectly fine during those years, just the usual aches and pains of getting older, but no new pills or sicknesses.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is accompanied by increased goal-directed activity and productivity (suggesting possible hypomanic/manic features of F41.1 Generalized Anxiety Disorder with prominent restlessness, versus F06.32 Mood disorder due to medical condition, versus R45.1 Nervousness), or if it's purely physical restlessness without increased accomplishment
doctor.question: Over this past year and a half when you've been feeling this restless and puttering around, have you actually gotten more done than you normally would—like more projects completed, more volunteer work accomplished, more things checked off your list—or does it feel like you're just moving around without really getting extra things finished?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about increased goal-directed activity (completing more projects or tasks), which is a symptom of mania/hypomania used for differential diagnosis, rather than a symptom in the provided ADHD profile.

patient.answer:
Well, that's a good question. You'd think with all this moving about I'd have the cleanest house in the county, wouldn't you? But no, not really. I'm always up and doing something, but it just feels like I'm spinning my wheels. I'll start organizing the hall closet, and then I'll find an old photo album, and before I know it, I'm sitting on the floor looking at pictures of my niece's wedding from 2004. It was a beautiful wedding, out in a garden with all these white roses. The bridesmaids wore lavender, which is a lovely color, but it washes some people out, don't you think? My sister—my niece's mother—insisted on it because it matched the invitations. She always was a stickler for coordination. When we were girls, she wouldn't even let her dolls wear mismatched shoes! She had this one doll, a Shirley Temple doll with those perfect little ringlets... oh, I loved that doll. 

But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I'm getting more done. I'm just puttering around, starting one thing and moving to another, and at the end of the day, the closet is still a mess and I'm just exhausted from all the pacing.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has experienced any head injury, stroke, or other acute neurological event in the past 1-2 years that could explain the sudden onset of akathisia-like symptoms, which would support F06.32 (anxiety disorder due to known physiological condition) over primary anxiety disorder F41.1

No, goodness no. I haven't fallen or hit my head, and certainly no strokes. My neighbor, though, Mr. Henderson—he had a stroke a few years back. It was terribly sad. He used to be out in his garden every single morning at 6 AM, rain or shine, tending to his tomatoes. He grew those big, beautiful heirloom ones, the ones that are sort of purple and green on the shoulders? Oh, they made the most wonderful sandwiches. Just a little mayonnaise, salt, and pepper on toasted sourdough. I used to buy my sourdough from that bakery on 4th Street, the one with the blue awning, but they closed down during the pandemic. Such a shame. The young couple who ran it were always so polite. The husband had this lovely singing voice, he'd hum while he kneaded the dough... 

But anyway, no, nothing like that for me. My head is perfectly fine, thank heavens. Just a bit too full of thoughts these days, I suppose!

doctor.intent: Distinguish between generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), which typically involves worry and anxiety symptoms, versus akathisia from a medical condition (F06.32) or anxiety unspecified (R45.1). patient.answer:
Well, no, not really. I don't think I've been grumpy or sad. I'm usually a pretty cheerful person, you know? Even when things get a bit chaotic with all this pacing. Speaking of pacing, I was walking back and forth in the living room just yesterday, and I noticed the most peculiar thing about my curtains. They're these heavy velvet drapes I bought back in the seventies—a deep maroon color. Velvet was so popular then, wasn't it? Everyone had velvet couches and velvet pillows. My sister even had a crushed velvet pantsuit in mustard yellow. She wore it to a fondue party we hosted in '74. Fondue was all the rage! We had cheese fondue first, and then chocolate for dessert. We dipped little pieces of pound cake and strawberries into the chocolate. It was terribly messy, but oh, so much fun. 

But no, to answer your question, my mood has been just fine. No sadness or grumpiness at all. Just the restlessness, really.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has akathisia (a medication side effect causing restlessness) by asking if she has noticed any involuntary movements or if her legs/body feel like they need to move, which would distinguish G25.3 from F41.1

patient.answer:
Well, no, it's not really an uncomfortable feeling in my legs. It's more just... a general feeling of needing to be doing something, you know? Like I just can't sit still. It's not like a cramp or a tingle or anything like that. Speaking of tingles, though, my feet used to fall asleep all the time when I'd sit on that old floral armchair we had in the den. It was a beautiful chair, really—had these big pink peonies on a cream background. I bought it at an estate sale over in Westlake. The woman running the sale was wearing the most fascinating brooch. It was shaped like a peacock, with real little emeralds for the eyes and sapphire tail feathers. I asked her about it, and she said it belonged to her great-aunt who used to travel all over Europe in the twenties. Imagine that! Traveling by ocean liner back then. They had those grand dining rooms with crystal chandeliers and a string quartet playing while you ate dinner. I've always wanted to go on a cruise, maybe up to Alaska to see the glaciers. I hear they're just breathtaking, though I suppose it would be terribly cold. You'd need a good, thick coat. My grandson bought me a lovely wool coat last Christmas, a deep forest green. It's so warm, but it's a bit heavy, to be honest. 

But anyway, no, my legs don't feel uncomfortable or anything. I just feel like I need to be up and moving around.

doctor.intent: Determine if the restlessness is akathisia (a medication side effect causing an irresistible urge to move) versus generalized anxiety disorder by asking about the subjective quality of the urge to move - whether it feels like an inner restlessness/compulsion that is difficult to resist, or more of a voluntary choice to stay active

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose it's a bit of both, really. I mean, I *could* sit still if I really forced myself, but it's just so much nicer to be doing something. It feels more like a preference, I think. I just don't like sitting idle. My mother was the exact same way, you know. She was always knitting or crocheting if she had to sit down. She made the most beautiful afghans. I still have the one she made for my wedding present—it's a lovely cream color with a sort of shell pattern. She used this very soft baby alpaca yarn she special-ordered from a catalog. Catalogs were so wonderful back then, weren't they? The Sears Roebuck catalog was thick as a telephone book! We used to circle the toys we wanted for Christmas in the Wish Book. I always wanted one of those Shirley Temple dolls with the little ringlets. My neighbor, little Patty, had one, and she had a whole wardrobe for it, little sailor dresses and patent leather shoes. The shoes even had tiny buckles! I don't know how they made things so small... 

But yes, to answer you, I just prefer to be up and about. It's not like I absolutely *have* to, I just... want to.

The patient's age (87), the non-anxiety-based nature of the restlessness, and the absence of classic anxiety or mood symptoms make akathisia (G25.3)—a medication-induced movement disorder—most likely, particularly given her 5-year history of antihypertensive medication.
